reasoning_traces.think: The foundational premise of BRIDGE lies in the observation that multimodal recommendation systems benefit from structured alignment rather than uniform consistency. The paper identifies a critical trade-off: moderate alignment enhances performance, while strong alignment introduces noise that suppresses specific recommendation variation. This insight leads to a dual-frequency decomposition strategy, separating shared structure (low-frequency) from private signals (high-frequency). The proposed framework integrates this spectral separation with behavior-guided evidence through three core modules: DFGE, BEN, and CRI. DFGE performs spectral decomposition of ID, visual, and textual features. BEN encodes co-user overlap into signed behavior evidence. CRI applies this evidence within a top-K candidate set to refine rankings. This modular architecture ensures that behavior signals are localized and integrated without disrupting the base model’s integrity. Empirical validation on Amazon Baby, Sports, and Electronics datasets demonstrates significant gains in Recall@20 and NDCG@20, confirming the efficacy of the dual-frequency approach. The theoretical grounding rests on spectral graph theory and Bayesian inference principles, where the low-frequency components represent stable, shared structures and high-frequency components encode personalized, dynamic signals. The framework thus balances generalization and personalization through frequency-aware integration. reasoning_traces.think: Chapter 2 explores how spectral frequency analysis of graph-smoothed representations enables dual-frequency integration for recommendation systems. The core insight is that low-frequency components capture shared structure across views, while high-frequency components retain discriminative ranking signals. This leads to a principled approach for balancing consistency and expressiveness in multi-modal recommendation. The paper introduces BRIDGE, which integrates these two types of information through a dual-frequency graph mechanism. The method dynamically weights contributions from different spectral bands based on their agreement and ranking utility. Empirically, this approach outperforms baselines that rely solely on either consistency or ranking signals. The key mathematical tool is the singular value decomposition (SVD) of graph-smoothed channel matrices, which defines frequency bands. These bands are then used to compute cross-view agreement and ranking signal strength. The framework supports both global and local calibration strategies, with behavior-derived corrections being particularly effective in sparse domains. The theoretical foundation lies in spectral graph theory and information theory, where frequency bands represent different levels of signal coherence and specificity. This allows for principled trade-offs between generalization and discrimination in recommendation tasks. The method constructs behavior graphs from training data alone, ensuring no leakage into validation or test sets. Inference quality improves with frequency regularization and content modality fusion, suggesting that both spectral and semantic dimensions contribute uniquely to recommendation accuracy. These findings support a principled framework for combining structured graph information with learned multimodal embeddings in recommender systems. reasoning_traces.think: This chapter introduces BRIDGE, a method that enhances recommendation systems by decomposing graph signals into low-frequency (stable cross-view structure) and high-frequency (sparse, item-specific variation) components. It uses an Information Bottleneck (IB) surrogate to control routing into these frequency bands and applies a frequency regularizer to preserve useful band geometry. The ablation studies demonstrate that both components are necessary: dropping either weakens the ranking signal. The decomposition itself is shown to be structural and largely independent of the basis used (Gram, DCT, random orthogonal). The key insight is that separating shared low-frequency evidence from high-frequency variation improves recall and NDCG by enabling better candidate coverage and re-ranking.
